{{distinguish|Geometry of numbers}}
'''Numerical algebraic geometry''' is a field of [[computational mathematics]], particularly [[computational algebraic geometry]], which uses methods from [[numerical analysis]] to study and manipulate the solutions of [[system of polynomial equations|systems of polynomial equations]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hauenstein |first1=Jonathan D. |last2=Sommese |first2=Andrew J. |title=What is numerical algebraic geometry? |journal=Journal of Symbolic Computation |date=March 2017 |volume=79 |pages=499–507 |doi=10.1016/j.jsc.2016.07.015|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www3.nd.edu/~cwample1/Preprints/intro2AlgGeom.pdf |last1=Sommese |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Verschelde |first2=Jan |last3=Wampler |first3=Charles W. |chapter=Introduction to Numerical Algebraic Geometry |editor-last1=Bronstein |editor-first1=Manuel |editor-last2=Cohen |editor-first2=Arjeh M. |editor-last3=Cohen |editor-first3=Henri |editor-last4=Eisenbud |editor-first4=David |editor-last5=Sturmfels |editor-first5=Bernd |editor-last6=Dickenstein |editor-first6=Alicia |editor-last7=Emiris |editor-first7=Ioannis Z. |title=Solving polynomial equations : foundations, algorithms, and applications |date=2005 |publisher=Springer-verlag |isbn=978-3-540-24326-7 |doi=10.1007/3-540-27357-3_8}}</ref><ref name=Macaulay2>{{Cite journal|last=Leykin|first=Anton|date=2000-01-01|title=Numerical algebraic geometry|url=http://msp.org/jsag/2011/3-1/p02.xhtml|journal=Journal of Software for Algebra and Geometry|volume=3|issue=1|pages=5–10|doi=10.2140/jsag.2011.3.5|issn=1948-7916|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Homotopy continuation==
{{see also|System of polynomial equations#Homotopy continuation method}}
The primary computational method used in numerical algebraic geometry is homotopy continuation, in which a [[homotopy]] is formed between two polynomial systems, and the isolated solutions (points) of one are continued to the other. This is a specialization of the more general method of [[numerical continuation]].

Let <math>z</math> represent the variables of the system.  By abuse of notation, and to facilitate the spectrum of ambient spaces over which one can solve the system, we do not use vector notation for <math>z</math>.  Similarly for the polynomial systems <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.

Current canonical notation calls the start system <math>g</math>, and the target system, i.e., the system to solve, <math>f</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sommese |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Wampler, II |first2=Charles W. |title=The numerical solution of systems of polynomials arising in engineering and science |date=2005 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-256-184-8}}</ref><ref name=Bertini>{{cite book |last1=Bates |first1=Daniel J. |last2=Sommese |first2=Andrew J. |last3=Hauenstein |first3=Jonathan D |last4=Wampler |first4=Charles W. |title=Numerically solving polynomial systems with Bertini |date=2013 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |isbn=978-1-61197-269-6}}</ref>  A very common homotopy, the straight-line homotopy, between <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> is
<math display="block"> H(z,t) = (1-t) f(z) + t g(z).</math>

In the above homotopy, one starts the path variable at <math>t_{\text{start}} = 1</math> and continues toward <math>t_{\text{end}} = 0</math>.  Another common choice is to run from <math>0</math> to <math>1</math>.  In principle, the choice is completely arbitrary.  In practice, regarding endgame methods for computing singular solutions using homotopy continuation, the target time being <math>0</math> can significantly ease analysis, so this perspective is here taken.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Tianran |last2=Li |first2=Tien-Yien |date=2015 |title=Homotopy continuation method for solving systems of nonlinear and polynomial equations |url=http://www.intlpress.com/site/pub/pages/journals/items/cis/content/vols/0015/0002/a001/ |journal=Communications in Information and Systems |language=en |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=276–277 |doi=10.4310/CIS.2015.v15.n2.a1|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Regardless of the choice of start and target times, the <math>H</math> ought to be formulated such that <math>H(z, t_{\text{start}}) = g(z)</math>, and <math>H(z, t_{\text{end}}) = f(z)</math>.

One has a choice in <math>g(z)</math>, including

* Roots of unity
* Total degree
* Polyhedral
* Multi-homogeneous

and beyond these, specific [[start system]]s that closely mirror the structure of <math>f</math> may be formed for particular systems.  The choice of start system impacts the computational time it takes to solve <math>f</math>, in that those that are easy to formulate (such as total degree) tend to have higher numbers of paths to track, and those that take significant effort (such as the polyhedral method) are much sharper.  There is currently no good way to predict which will lead to the quickest time to solve.{{Citation needed|reason=need a source indicating this please|date=January 2017}}

Actual continuation is typically done using [[predictor–corrector method]]s, with additional features as implemented.  Predicting is done using a standard [[ordinary differential equation|ODE]] predictor method, such as [[Runge–Kutta]], and correction often uses Newton–Raphson iteration.

Because <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are polynomial, homotopy continuation in this context is theoretically guaranteed to compute all solutions of <math>f</math>, due to [[Theorem of Bertini|Bertini's theorem]].  However, this guarantee is not always achieved in practice, because of issues arising from limitations of the modern computer, most namely finite precision.  That is, despite the strength of the probability-1 argument underlying this theory, without using a priori certified tracking methods, some paths may fail to track perfectly for various reasons.

==Witness set==
A witness set 
<math>W</math> is a data structure used to describe [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]]. The witness set for an affine variety that is equidimensional consists of three pieces of information. The first piece of information is a system of equations <math>F</math>. These equations define the algebraic variety <math>{\mathbf V}(F)</math> that is being studied. The second piece of information is a linear space <math>\mathcal{L}</math>. The dimension of <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is the codimension of <math>{\mathbf V}(F)</math>, and chosen to intersect <math>{\mathbf V}(F)</math> transversely. The third piece of information is the list of points in the intersection <math>\mathcal{L}\cap{\mathbf V}(F)</math>. This intersection has finitely many points and the number of points is the degree of the algebraic variety <math>{\mathbf V}(F)</math>. Thus, witness sets encode the answer to the first two questions one asks about an algebraic variety: What is the dimension, and what is the degree? Witness sets also allow one to perform a numerical irreducible decomposition, component membership tests, and component sampling. This makes witness sets a good description of an algebraic variety.

==Certification==

Solutions to polynomial systems computed using numerical algebraic geometric methods can be [[Numerical certification|certified]], meaning that the approximate solution is "correct".  This can be achieved in several ways, either a priori using a certified tracker,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Beltrán|first1=Carlos|last2=Leykin|first2=Anton|date=2012-03-01|title=Certified Numerical Homotopy Tracking|journal=Experimental Mathematics|volume=21|issue=1|pages=69–83|doi=10.1080/10586458.2011.606184|issn=1058-6458|arxiv=0912.0920|s2cid=2889087}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Beltrán|first1=Carlos|last2=Leykin|first2=Anton|date=2013-02-01|title=Robust Certified Numerical Homotopy Tracking|journal=Foundations of Computational Mathematics|language=en|volume=13|issue=2|pages=253–295|doi=10.1007/s10208-013-9143-2|issn=1615-3375|arxiv=1105.5992|s2cid=32990257}}</ref> or a posteriori by showing that the point is, say, in the basin of convergence for Newton's method.<ref name = "alphaCertified">{{cite journal |last1=Hauenstein |first1=Jonathan D. |last2=Sottile |first2=Frank |title=Algorithm 921: alphaCertified: Certifying Solutions to Polynomial Systems |journal=ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software |date=August 2012 |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1145/2331130.2331136|s2cid=13821271 }}</ref>

==Software==

Several software packages implement portions of the theoretical body of numerical algebraic geometry. These include, in alphabetic order:

* alphaCertified<ref name="alphaCertified" />
* Bertini <ref name=Bertini/>
* Hom4PS<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chen |first1=T. |last2=Lee |first2=T. L. |last3=Li |first3=T. Y. |chapter=Hom4PS-3: A Parallel Numerical Solver for Systems of Polynomial Equations Based on Polyhedral Homotopy Continuation Methods |pages=183–190 |editor-last1=Hong |editor-first1=H. |editor-last2=Yap |editor-first2=C. |title=Mathematical software -- ICMS 2014 : 4th International Congress, Seoul, South Korea, August 5-9, 2014. Proceedings |date=2014 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-44199-2_30 |isbn=978-3-662-44199-2 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-44199-2_30 |accessdate=28 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hom4PS Team |title=Featured Products |url=http://www.hom4ps3.org/store/c1/Featured_Products.html |website=Hom4PS-3 |publisher=Michigan State University |accessdate=28 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref>
* HomotopyContinuation.jl<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Breiding |first1=Paul |last2= Timme |first2=Sascha |eprint=1711.10911v2 |title=HomotopyContinuation.jl: A package for homotopy continuation in Julia |class=cs.MS |date=May 2018 }}</ref>
* [[Macaulay2]] (core implementation of homotopy tracking and <code>NumericalAlgebraicGeometry</code><ref name=Macaulay2/> package)
* [[MiNuS]]: Optimized C++ framework for fast homotopy continuation. Fastest solver for certain 100-320 degree square problems to date.
* PHCPack<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Verschelde |first1=Jan |title=Algorithm 795: PHCpack: a general-purpose solver for polynomial systems by homotopy continuation |journal=ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software |date=1 June 1999 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=251–276 |doi=10.1145/317275.317286|s2cid=15485257 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
